name: Kannada
variety: Standard Kannada (educated speech of the Mysore and Bangalore area), formal style
sources: Sridhar, S. N. (1990). Kannada. London: Routledge (Descriptive Grammars).
Schiffman, Harold F. (1983). A Reference Grammar of Spoken Kannada. Seattle: University of Washington Press.
Steever, Sanford B. (1998). Kannada. In Steever (ed.), The Dravidian Languages. London: Routledge.
Upadhyaya, U. P. (1972). Kannada Phonetic Reader. Mysore: Central Institute of Indian Languages.
Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju (2003). The Dravidian Languages. Cambridge University Press.
contrasts: vowel length for five vowel qualities
voiced versus voiceless stops in all vocabulary; aspirated and breathy voiced stops in Sanskrit and other loans, kept in educated formal speech and mostly lost colloquially
dental versus retroflex stops; alveolar versus retroflex nasal and lateral
/ɲ ŋ/ occur almost only before homorganic stops
/f z/ in Perso-Arabic and English loans; /ʃ/ and /ʂ/ are merged by most speakers
allophony: word-initial /e eː/ take a [j] on-glide and /o oː/ a [w] on-glide
the written nasal (anusvara) is homorganic with a following stop ([ŋ ɲ ɳ n̪ m]) and is [m] word-finally
/r/ is a tap [ɾ] between vowels and a trill when geminate or emphatic
/ʋ/ is a labiodental approximant, [w]-like before rounded vowels
short /a/ is centralised [ɐ] or [ʌ]; final short vowels are short and lax
aspirated and breathy voiced stops are pronounced without aspiration in colloquial speech
colloquial speech deletes short vowels of medial syllables, creating clusters (literary māḍuttēne, spoken māḍtīni 'I do')
English loans may keep [æː] and [ɔː] as extra vowel qualities
phonotactics: words of the formal language end in a vowel; consonant-final stems and loanwords add the enunciative vowel -u (bassu 'bus')
initial clusters occur in Sanskrit and English loans
medial clusters are chiefly geminates and homorganic nasal plus stop in the formal language
retroflex /ɳ ɭ/ do not occur word-initially

stress.type: no lexical stress; weak fixed prominence, not contrastive
stress.rule: A slight prominence falls on the first syllable of the word.
stress.cues: phrase-level pitch and slight lengthening; no reduction of vowel quality in the formal language

rhythm.vowel_reduction: none in the formal language; colloquial speech deletes short medial vowels
rhythm.notes: Syllable-timed is the traditional label. Because vowel and consonant length are contrastive, syllable duration follows the number of moras. No instrumental rhythm classification or nPVI value is cited here.

length.notes: Long vowels are roughly twice as long as short vowels and geminate closures roughly twice as long as single ones (approximate ratios; no exact figures cited).

intonation.declarative: non-final phrases start low and rise toward their end; the final phrase, normally the verb, falls to low
intonation.yes_no_question: marked by the clitic -ā on the verb or on the questioned word, with statement word order; pitch rises on the lengthened clitic vowel
intonation.wh_question: question word stays in place and carries the main peak, followed by a fall to low
intonation.continuation: rise to a high boundary at the end of non-final phrases and non-finite clauses
intonation.accent_shape: low at the start of the phrase with a rise to its right edge (LH); no pitch accents tied to lexical stress
intonation.notes: Instrumental work on Kannada intonation is sparse; this follows the reference grammars and the general pattern described for the neighbouring Dravidian languages.

phonation: breathy voiced (voiced aspirated) stops /bʱ d̪ʱ ɖʱ dʒʱ ɡʱ/ in learned vocabulary

problems: ರ /r/ imports base1/r, the English approximant [ɹ] (IPA output [mˈɐɹɐ] for ಮರ), instead of a tap or trill
in the phoneme table short a carries the lng flag while the long vowels do not; the table is headed 'these are only guesses'
no on-glides for word-initial e and o
stress is fixed on the first syllable with stress-accent settings, and automatic secondary stress can fall on a short vowel next to an unstressed long one (ಕರ್ನಾಟಕ gives [kˈɐrnaːʈˌɐkɐ])
the obsolete letter ೞ (historical retroflex approximant, now /ɭ/) is read as [fa]
good: anusvara is homorganic before stops and [m] otherwise
vowel length (short 110 to 130, long 270 to 300 in table units) and geminates (doubled consonant phonemes) are kept
dental, retroflex, aspirated and breathy voiced stops come from the Hindi base table; nukta forms give [z] and [f]

notes: Kannada is diglossic like Tamil, though less sharply. Written text follows the formal language, in which every vowel is pronounced; the colloquial deletions are listed for reference only.
